parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State two ways in which the first law of thermodynamics describes that the internal energy of a system may be changed.

markscheme_points.text: thermal energy supplied to / removed from system

hints: Hint 1: Think about internal energy as energy stored inside the system. For it to change, energy must cross the boundary of the system in some form - what are the two broad ways energy can be transferred in or out?
Hint 2: One way involves a mechanical push or pull through a distance when volume changes, the other way involves a temperature difference driving energy flow. Name both processes.
parts.proper_answer: 1. By work done on the system or by the system. 2. By heating - thermal energy supplied to the system or removed from the system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember What The First Law Means**
Think of internal energy $U$ as the total of all the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules in the system. Because energy is conserved, $U$ can only change if energy comes in from outside or goes out to outside.

Step 2: **The Two Transfer Routes**
There are only two routes in the first law: $$\Delta U = q + w$$ where $q$ is the thermal energy transferred by heating (positive if supplied to the system) and $w$ is the work done on the system (positive if done on the system, negative if done by the system to expand). So state both: work done and heating.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Use the first law of thermodynamics to explain why a bicycle pump gets hot when it is used to pump up a tyre quickly.

markscheme_points.text: no thermal energy transferred to / from system (due to lack of time)
work is done on the gas to compress it / to decrease its volume
internal energy increases so temperature increases

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the word quickly. If compression happens very fast, is there time for thermal energy to flow through the pump walls to or from the surroundings?
Hint 2: Think about what your hand does to the gas. When the piston moves in and the volume decreases, is work being done on the gas or by the gas?

Hint 3: Link the change in stored energy to what you feel. If internal energy must increase and there is no heat loss, what must happen to the average molecular kinetic energy and hence the temperature?
parts.proper_answer: Pumping is rapid so no thermal energy is transferred to or from the gas. Work is done on the gas to compress it and decrease its volume. By the first law, internal energy increases, so average molecular kinetic energy and temperature increase and the pump gets hot.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why No Heating Term**
Because the pumping is quick, there is almost no time for thermal energy to conduct through the walls. So this is effectively adiabatic: $$q = 0$$ No heat enters or leaves during the stroke.

Step 2: **Work Done On The Gas**
You push the piston in with a force through a distance, compressing the gas to a smaller volume. That means work is done on the gas, so $w$ is positive. From the first law $$\Delta U = q + w$$ with $q = 0$, $\Delta U = w > 0$.

Step 3: **From Internal Energy To Hot Pump**
A larger $U$ for an ideal-like gas means larger total molecular kinetic energy. Temperature is a measure of average random kinetic energy per molecule, so temperature rises. The hot gas then warms the metal pump by conduction, which is why you feel it get hot.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: With reference to molecular energies, explain why the temperature of water remains at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ when it vaporises in a kettle, even though it is being heated.

markscheme_points.text: (heating causes) potential energy of molecules to increase
kinetic energy of molecules unchanged so temperature unchanged

hints: Hint 1: Start by splitting internal energy into its two parts. Which part controls temperature, and which part controls how tightly molecules are bound together?
Hint 2: Picture liquid turning to vapour. What happens to the average spacing between water molecules and the forces between them?
Hint 3: If all the incoming heating goes into pulling molecules apart against attraction, what is left over to increase molecular speeds and temperature?
parts.proper_answer: During vaporisation molecular separation increases. Supplied thermal energy increases the electric potential energy of the molecules in overcoming intermolecular attraction. Average molecular kinetic energy is unchanged, so temperature remains at 100 degrees C.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Split Internal Energy In Two**
Remember $$U = E_{k} + E_{p}$$ where $E_{k}$ is total random kinetic energy and $E_{p}$ is total intermolecular potential energy. Temperature depends only on the average $E_{k}$ per molecule, not on $E_{p}$.

Step 2: **What Boiling Really Does**
In liquid water molecules are close and attracted to each other. To form vapour they must be pulled far apart against those attractive forces. That requires work at molecular level, so molecular potential energy $E_{p}$ increases.

Step 3: **Why Temperature Stays Constant**
The thermal energy supplied by the kettle goes entirely into increasing $E_{p}$, not into increasing $E_{k}$. Since average kinetic energy stays the same, temperature stays at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ until all liquid has vaporised, even though heating continues.
